lead: A word needs a numeric form before a classifier or a similarity search can use it. One-hot encoding gives each word its own position in a long vector of zeros and a single one. Dense word vectors give each word a short list of real numbers. The dense geometry can place cricket near bat and far from monsoon, even when the words never share a sentence. Search, clustering, sentiment models and neural NLP all begin from such representations.
prereq: You need: 5.1 term vectors and basic vector arithmetic (dot product, length).

blocks.text: Let V be the vocabulary, the set of distinct words the system knows, and let |V| be its size. Number the words 1 to |V|. The one-hot vector e_w for word w has dimension |V| and Euclidean length 1. Every entry is 0 except position w, which is 1. In a vocabulary of 50,000 words, each vector has 49,999 zeros. The vector is sparse.

Different words put their 1 in different positions. Their dot product is 0 and the angle between them is 90°. Cosine similarity, which depends only on angle, is therefore 0 for every pair of different one-hot words. Cricket and bat look as unrelated as cricket and ball. The representation stores identity, not meaning. One-hot vectors still work as input to the classifiers in 5.2; the classifier learns which positions matter.

blocks.where: a and b are vectors; a · b = Σᵢ aᵢbᵢ is the dot product; |a| = √(a · a) is the length. Cosine is 1 for same direction, 0 for perpendicular, −1 for opposite.

blocks.text: Build a co-occurrence matrix M from a corpus. Pick a window, for example 5 words to the left and 5 to the right. For every occurrence of a word w, count each context word c in the window. M[w, c] is that count. Rows are words, columns are context words. The matrix is large and sparse.

Raw counts are dominated by frequent words such as the. Positive pointwise mutual information (PPMI) compares the observed count with what chance would give. Estimate probabilities from the matrix: P(w,c)=count(w,c)/T, P(w)=row total/T, P(c)=column total/T, where T is the sum of all counts. Then PMI(w,c)=log₂(P(w,c)/(P(w)P(c))). PPMI(w,c)=max(PMI(w,c),0). Negative PMI means the pair occurs less than chance; PPMI sets it to 0.

blocks.where: M is the PPMI matrix; U and V have orthonormal columns; Σ is diagonal with singular values in decreasing order. Keep the k largest singular values. The dense vector for word w is row w of U_k Σ_k, a list of k real numbers.

blocks.text: Singular value decomposition (SVD) compresses the matrix. This use of SVD on a word-context count matrix is a count-based distributional method; the same idea applied to a term-document matrix is latent semantic analysis (LSA). Some syllabi call the whole idea vector semantics or distributed representations. A word's vector now depends on the company it keeps. The link between context and similarity is developed in 5.7.

Dense vectors are short, for example 100 or 300 numbers. They are not one-hot and not interpretable one entry per word. Their geometry matters. Words used in similar contexts get vectors with small angles. Compare them with cosine, not by checking equality.

Cosine ignores vector length. If you also need distance, normalize each vector to unit length first: x̂ = x/|x|. Then the dot product of two unit vectors equals their cosine, and Euclidean distance is √(2−2cos). This avoids a long vector looking far away only because of scale.

Dense vectors help when labelled data is small, because they share statistical strength across similar words. In document clustering, average the dense vectors of the document's words, then cluster the averages; see 5.7. For unknown words, use a reserved unknown token; do not silently use a zero vector.

figure.caption: The same two words in two encodings. One-hot puts their 1s in different positions, so the dot product is 0 and the cosine is 0; the dense vectors give dot 0.56 and cosine ≈ 0.94.

spec.title: One-hot vs dense for cricket and bat
spec.aria: Flow from the words cricket and bat to their one-hot vectors [1,0,0] and [0,1,0], which give cosine 0, and to their dense vectors [0.8,0.2] and [0.6,0.4], which give cosine about 0.94.

examples.question: Vocabulary = {cricket, bat, ball}. One-hot: cricket=[1,0,0], bat=[0,1,0]. Dense: cricket=[0.8,0.2], bat=[0.6,0.4]. Compute the one-hot cosine and the dense cosine between cricket and bat.
steps: The vocabulary has 3 words, so each one-hot vector has dimension 3. cricket has its 1 in position 1: [1,0,0]. bat has its 1 in position 2: [0,1,0].
One-hot dot product = 1×0 + 0×1 + 0×0 = 0. Each one-hot vector has length 1 because it has one non-zero entry equal to 1.
examples.answer: One-hot cosine = 0; dense cosine ≈ 0.942 (0.9417 to four decimal places).
examples.check:
import math
dot = 0.8 * 0.6 + 0.2 * 0.4
nc = math.sqrt(0.8**2 + 0.2**2)
nb = math.sqrt(0.6**2 + 0.4**2)
cos = dot / (nc * nb)
print(round(dot, 4))
print(round(nc, 4))
print(round(nb, 4))
print(round(cos, 4))

traps: A one-hot vector's dimension is |V|, the vocabulary size, so all words use the same number of entries. Its Euclidean length is always 1, because exactly one entry equals 1.
Cosine similarity of two different one-hot vectors is 0. That does not mean the words are unrelated; it means the representation cannot express relatedness.
PPMI replaces negative PMI with 0 after taking the log. Do not clip counts before the log.

SVD gives U, Σ and Vᵀ, and row w of U_kΣ_k is row w of U_k scaled by σ_w. Cosine is unaffected by that scaling, but dot products and Euclidean distances are not; state which you use before using either.
Dense vector similarity is not Euclidean distance unless vectors are normalized. Cosine is an angle, not a distance.

quiz.q: What is the dimension of the one-hot vector for a word in a vocabulary of 5000 words, and what is its Euclidean length?
quiz.a: Dimension 5000: one entry equal to 1 and 4999 entries equal to 0. Euclidean length 1, because √(1²) = 1.

quiz.q: Why can cosine similarity not separate cricket and bat when both are one-hot vectors?
quiz.a: Different one-hot vectors have 1s in different positions, so their dot product is 0. Their angle is 90°, so cosine is 0 for every pair of different words.

quiz.q: Compute the dot product of a=[0.8,0.2] and b=[0.6,0.4].
Two dense vectors have cosine 0.99 but large Euclidean distance. Explain how both can be true.
quiz.a: Cosine measures angle only. If one vector is much longer than the other, their distance can be large even when the angle is small. Normalize both vectors before using distance.

quiz.q: What does PPMI do to negative PMI values, and why?
quiz.a: PPMI sets negative PMI to 0. A negative value means the pair occurs less than chance; clipping keeps the matrix nonnegative and sparse.

quiz.q: Why apply SVD to a word-context count matrix instead of using raw counts as vectors?
quiz.a: Raw counts are sparse and dominated by frequent words. SVD reduces dimensionality and noise, giving short dense vectors whose geometry captures similarity.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern systems learn dense vectors by prediction rather than counting; Word2Vec and GloVe are covered in 5.6. Contextual models such as BERT give a different vector for a word in each sentence; see Unit 6. In industry, embeddings power search, recommendation and deduplication. Useful search terms: latent semantic analysis, PPMI, singular value decomposition, embedding evaluation.
